failures.criterion: F4/F5 as the PR and the doc state them: the clean-up is a trap that runs on any exit short of SIGKILL, so a role that pastes the published block is covered when its command stops; the doc tells a role which stops leave the Job for the recovery line (docs/kubernetes.md:2930-2955, and the block's own comment at 2924-2925).
failures.evidence: The way a role's command actually stops is its own bash tool, and the tool's stop is a SIGKILL in practice, which the doc does not say. Measured 2026-10-25 11:42-11:47Z from the tester's role container at head 16ed0a2f: (1) the rendered block, unmodified, run through the role's bash tool (`eval "$(cat r-S1.sh)"`, i.e. pasted, which runs `bash "$sequence"`) with a tool timeout of 40 s: the tool printed `workload: infra-215-postgres-39cea3`, the Job and Service created, `error: interrupted` from the Ready wait, then `[Command timed out after 40 seconds]`; 15 s later the sequence's bash was gone, the Job and Service still existed with no deletionTimestamp and the pod Pending, so the trap never reached its delete; the doc's recovery lines removed it (0.4 s, wait exit 0, listing empty). (2) Why: a probe with a foreground python child logging every 20 ms after a catchable signal, run under a bash parent in the bash tool with a 4 s timeout ($TMPDIR/infra215/test/probe3.py, probe4.log): the child got SIGTERM at the deadline and was killed about 70 ms later (four `alive` lines); a bash with INT/TERM/HUP/QUIT/PIPE and EXIT traps writing to a file (probe.sh, probe2.sh) logged none of them. So the tool sends SIGTERM to the command's process group and SIGKILL some tens of milliseconds later, far less than the trap's first diagnostic `kubectl get` and its seconds-long foreground delete. The doc measures only stops sent by hand to the script's group or bash (vrun.py ran the block under setsid nohup, outside the tool), says `A SIGKILL, or the role's pod going away, runs no trap`, and never tells a role that its bash tool's timeout is that case, so a role whose call times out reads `[Command timed out …]` and has no reason to run the recovery line, leaving 4 CPU on the shared quota for up to an hour. [INFERENCE, not measured: an aborted tool call or a turn the daemon interrupts uses the same kill.] Needed: the doc says what a tool timeout or abort does to the sequence and gives a role the way to run it so its clean-up survives (for example a tool timeout above the sequence's own bound of 120 s + 300 s + 60 s plus the work, or running it detached from the tool's process group and following its output), and states the recovery line is the answer to a timed-out call; the fix is then driven through the bash tool, as here. No red test: this is prose plus cluster behaviour, the repository has no suite that can run the block against a cluster, and a test asserting the doc's text is what the repository's testing rules forbid; the reproduction is the bash-tool run above.
